la:adj:bibulus.gloss: fond of drinking; drinking readily or freely; frequently thirsty; bibulous
senses: fond of drinking; drinking readily or freely; frequently thirsty; bibulous
that sucks in or absorbs; absorbent, porous, bibulous
ready to hear; thirsty to listen; listening
la:adj:bibulus.html:
bĭbŭlus, a, um, adj.
1. bibo
.
Lit., drinking readily, freely (poet. or in postAug. prose): bibulus Falerni,: potores,.—More freq.,
Transf., of inanim. things, that sucks in or absorbs moisture: harena,sand that imbibes, drinks up moisture,; ; : lapis,a stone that absorbs moisture, (qui harenarius vocatur, Serv.); : litus, (17), 139: favilla,: radix,: talaria,moistened,: medulla,: ollae bibulae aut male coctae,: papyrus,growing in moist places,: charta,blotting-paper,; cf. : taenia papyri,: nubes, (cf. 1. bibo, B. 1.): lanae, absorbing or taking color, (v. poto).—
Trop., of hearing (cf. 1. bibo, II.): aures,ready to hear, listening,.

la:adj:biduus.html:
bidŭus, a, um, adj.
bis-dies
,
continuing two days, of two days; as adj. only once, with tempus, , where tempus is prob. to be omitted; v. Weissenb. ad loc. But very freq. and class. as subst.: bīdŭum, ii, n. (sc. tempus), a period or space of two days, two days: sinito biduom aut triduom consudent (oves),: biduum supererat,; ; Planc. ap. : in castra quae aberant bidui (sc. spatio),; ; cf. : eximant unum aliquem diem aut summum biduum ex mense,: rus ibo: ibi hoc me macerabo biduum,; ; ; ; ; ; : supplicationes in biduum decretae,: per biduum,; Quint. prooem. 7: per insequens biduum,: uno die longior mensis aut biduo,: biduo et duabus noctibus Adrumetum pervenit,: biduo post,; so : post biduum,; : biduo continenti,; ; .

la:verb:bibo.html:
bĭbo, bĭbi (post-class.
part. fut. bĭbĭtūrus, ; ; ; ; part. perf. bĭbĭtus, a, um, Cael. Aur. Chron. 4, 3, 60; ; Aem. Mac. c. de Porro; ; inf. apocop. biber, Cato, Titin., and Fannii Annal. ap. ), 3, v. a.
root bi; Gr. πι-, πίνω, πέπωκα; whence Lat. poto, as if from po; Sanscr. pī; Slav. piti; Lith. pota
, to drink (usually from thirst, a natural want; poto, to drink from passion, habit, etc.; but poto is occasionally used of water, etc., e. g. ; cf.: bibere naturae est, potare luxuriae,. 74; and the partt. potus and potatus are regularly used instead of the partt. of bibo).
With acc.
Of the liquid drunk: per aestatem boves aquam bonam et liquidam bibant semper curato,: jejunus heminam bibito,: si voles vinum Choum bibere, licebit bibas,: eapse merum condidicit bibere; foribus dat aquam quam bibant,: vicit vinum quod bibi,: Darius in fugā cum aquam turbidam bibisset,: patrono malo suadebat ut mulsum frigidum biberet,: viveret, nisi illud (i. e. venenum) bibisset,: bibo aquam,: cur apud te vinum aetate tuā vetustius bibitur?: nisi Hy. mettia mella Falerno Ne biberis diluta,: et Veientani bibitur faex crassa rubelli,: lac bibere,to suck,; ; .—Also nutricem bibere (i. e. lac de nutrice), .—Poet.; Caecubam... Tu bibes uvam (i. e. vinum),: in usu radix tantum duabus drachmis bibenda (i. e. sucus radicis),.—
Pocula or cyathos bibere.
Poet., = vinum (cf. πίνειν κρατῆρας): tristia cum multo pocula felle bibat,: ipse bibebam Sobria suppositā pocula victor aquā,: plura pocula = plus vini,; so, nomismata and aera,.—
Of the number of cups drunk at a merry-making: vide quot cyathos bibimus: St. Tot quot digiti sunt tibi in manu, .—Esp. of the custom of drinking names, i. e. as many cups as there are letters in a name proposed; the number is frequently expressed by fractional parts of the as (uncia = a cyathus; quincunx = 5 cyathi, etc.): quincunces et sex cyathos bessemque bibamus, Gaius ut fiat, Julius, et Proculus,: crebros ergo licet bibas trientes,: diluti bibis unciam Falerni, (cf. with potare: sextantes et deunces,).—Hence, nomen bibere, Julium, etc., bibere: ut jugulem curas, nomen utrumque bibam,: Laevia sex cyathis, septem Justina bibatur, Quinque Lycas, Lyde quattuor, Ida tribus,: Astyanacta bibes,.—
Fluvium, undam, pruinas bibere (poet.).
= aquam ex flumine bibere: priusquam Pabula gustassent Trojae Xanthumque bibissent,: jam crassus torrens bibitur tamen,: puram bibis amnibus undam,.—
Trop., to arrive at the region of the river: non illum nostri possunt mutare labores, Nec si... Hebrumque bibamus Sithoniasque nives... subeamus (i. e. si Thraciam adeamus),: ante... Aut Ararim Parthus bibet, aut Germania Tigrim Quam, etc.,sooner will the Parthians come to Germany, or the Germans to the country of the Parthians,: turbaque Phasiacam Graia bibistis aquam,.—Hence,
Qui flumen bibunt, = the inhabitants of the country through which the river passes: qui Tiberim Fabarimque bibunt,: qui profundum Danubium bibunt,: qui Nilum ex ipso protinus ore bibunt,: populosque bibentes Euphraten,: qui te, Nile, bibit, Claud. Prob. et Olybr. 38.—So of an inland sea: caesamque bibens Maeotin Alanus,.—Of a single person: extremum Tanaim si biberes, Lyce,.—Similarly, montium pruinas bibere, of the rivers fed by a mountain range: amniumque... quicunque Odrysias bibunt pruinas,: fluvios qui... Alpinasque bibunt de more pruinas, Claud. Prob. et Olybr. 255.—
Bibere aquas, to be drowned: neu bibat aequoreas naufragus hostis aquas,.—Transf., of ships, to founder, to be wrecked: o utinam... Argo funestas pressa bibisset aquas! .—
Sanguinem or cruorem bibere.
Sanguinem, in a figurative sense, = sanguinem sitire: cujus sanguinem (Antonium) non bibere censeatis? (sitire, animo bibere),.—
Cruorem bibere, to draw blood, to kill: hasta virgineum alte bibit acta cruorem,; .—
Transf. to things other than liquids.
Of concrete things: dixit et ardentes avido bibit ore favillas, breathed in, drew in (of the sparks of a funeral pyre), : vigilandae noctes et fuligo lucubrationum bibenda,inhale,.—
Figuratively, of abstract things.
= cupideaudire, legere: pugnas et exactos tyrannos... bibit aure vulgus,eagerly listens to,: incipe: suspensis auribus ista bibam,: hinc ille justitiae haustus bibat, imbibe (by reading) the love of justice, : illa divino fruitur sermone parentis, maternosque bibit mores, 231.—
To imbibe, be affected with: infelix Dido, longumque bibebat amorem,: totisque novum bibit ossibus ignem,the fire of love,.—
To draw out, exhaust: nudae illae artes omnem sucum ingenii bibunt, Quint. prooem. 24.—
To swallow, i. e. forget: quamquam ego vinum bibo, mandata hau consuevi simul bibere una,. —
Transf., of inanim. subjects, to absorb liquids, draw, imbibe them: id si feceris metreta oleum non bibet,. —So trop.: claudite jam rivos... sat prata biberunt,: inriguumque bibant violaria fontem,: quae (terra) bibit humorem,absorbs moisture,: amphora fumum bibere instituta,: mista bibunt molles lacrimis unguenta favillae,: tunc bibit irriguus fertilis hortus aquas,: lanarum nigrae nullum colorem bibunt,take no color,; so, candorem (i. e. colorem candidum) bibere,: arcus bibit (aquas) and nubes bibunt (aquas), the rainbow, the clouds draw water (according to a popular belief among the ancients): cur bibit arcus aquas? (4, 4), 32: et bibit ingens Arcus,.—And, jestingly, of an old woman given to drink: ecce autem, bibit arcus; hercle, credo, hodie pluet, (44): unde aures nubesque bibunt atque imbrifer arcus,.—So with object understood: bibite, festivae fores,with reference to the wine spilled,: palma toto anno bibere amat, i. e. aquam,.—
Absol. (the obj. acc. understood).
Sc. aquam: nec sitis est exstincta priusquam vita bibendo (of those seized by the plague),.—
Of liquids in general: numquam sitiens biberat,: edendi mihi erit bibendique finis desideria naturae restinguere,: ut nec bibant sine ambitione, nec edant,: conducit inter cibos bibere,: vino debemus homines quod soli animalium non sitientes bibimus,.—
Esp. of wine: es, bibe, animo obsequere mecum,: quamquam illud est dulce, esse et bibere,: jam diu factum postquam bibimus: nimis diu sicci sumus,; : decet luxuriosum bibendo mori,: ut jejuni biberent,—Pass. impers. bibitur, they drink, he drinks, people drink: dies noctisque estur, bibitur,: ab tertiā horā bibebatur, ludebatur, vomebatur,: bibitur usque eo dum de solio ministretur,.—
With adverbs or adverbial phrases.
Of manner: jucundius bibere,; : large,: fit invitatio ut Graeco more biberetur, i. e. propinando,.—
With num. adv. denoting the number of cups: jam bis bibisse oportuit,: sic ago, semel bibo,: plus quam deciens, Sextiliane, bibis,: quare bis deciens, Sextiliane bibis?.—
With abl. or prep. and abl.
Of the liquid, river, etc.: de eo vino... bibito ante cenam,: a fonte bibatur...

an lacu, : ab amne,: ex aquā,: ex fonte,.—

Of the vessel.
Abl.: gemmā, i. e. poculo ex gemmā facto,: caelato = e poculo caelato,: conchā,: fictilibus,: testā,: vitro,; : ossibus humanorum capitum,.—And bibere understood: poscunt majoribus poculis, i. e. bibi,.—
With ex: ex solido auro, L. Varius ap. : e gemmā,.—
With in: hac licet in gemmā bibas,: in Priami calathis,: in auro,: in argento potorio,: in ossibus capitum,.—
Particular phrases.
Bibe si bibis = bibe nunc, si omnino bibere vis, a formula urging to drink, ; (cf.: age, si quid agis,).—
Dare bibere, to give to drink, a Grecism, perh. only in the foll. passages: date illi biber, Titin ap. P. (Com. Rel. v. 78 Rib.): jubebat biber dari, Fann. Ann. ib: bibere da usque plenis cantharis, (45): quod jussi ei dari bibere,; cf.: ut Jovi bibere ministraret,: ut bibere sibi juberet dari,: cf.: dare with subj.: tum vos date bibat tibicini,.—And with rel. and subj.: nimium dabat quod biberem,: dat aquam quam bibant,.—
Prov.: aut bibat aut abeat, taken from the Greek banquets, in which the chairman (arbiter bibendi,) could demand unconditional submission to the drinking laws (ἢ πῖθι, ἢ ἄπιθι), .

la:adv:bis.gloss: twice, two times, on two occasions, in two ways
senses: twice, two times, on two occasions, in two ways
la:adv:bis.html:
bis, adv. num.
for duis, from duo; like bellum from duellum, Paul. ex Müll.; cf. , and the letter B
,
twice, at two times, on two occasions, in two ways, = δίς (very freq. in prose and poetry).
In gen.: inde ad nos elisa bis advolat (imago),; ; ; ; ; ; : non semel sed bis,: semel aut bis,: bis ac saepius,; : bis mori,: bis consul, who has been twice consul in all (diff. from iterum consul, who is a second time consul), ; ; ; ; ; ; 25, 5, 3; cf. ; .—Sometimes (among later writers) for iterum, now a second time: bis consul,; Prid. Kal. Febr.; Coll. Leg. Mos. et Rom. 1, § 11.—
Bis is followed by,
Semel ... iterum, : bis dimicavit: semel ad Dyrrhachium, iterum in Hispaniā,; so ; ; ; ; cf. Wolf, ejusd. .—
Primo... rursus, ; .—
Et rursus, without a preceding primo, ; .—
Transf., doubly, twofold, in two ways, in a twofold manner: bis periit amator, ab re atque animo simul,: nam qui amat cui odio ipsus est, bis facere stulte duco; laborem inanem ipsus capit, et illi molestiam adfert,: in unā civitate bis improbus fuisti, cum et remisisti quod non oportebat, et accepisti quod non licebat,: in quo bis laberis, primum, quod... deinde, quod, etc.,: inopi beneficium bis dat qui dat celeriter, Publ. Syr. v. 235 Rib.: bis gratum est, ib.: bis est mori alterius arbitrio mori, ib.—
Particular connections.
Bis in die, mense, anno, etc., or bis die, mense, anno, etc., twice a day, month, year, etc.; cf. Oud.; ; : bis in die,; ; : bis die,; ; ; ; ; , n. 2; ; cf. cotidie,: in mense,; : in anno,: anno,.—
With other numerals, and particularly with distributives (class. in prose and poetry): bis binos,; : bis quinos dies,; ; : bis senos dies,: bis septeni,: bis octoni,: bis deni,; ; : bis quinquageni,: bis milies, ; Auct. B. Afr. 90; .—
Esp., with cardinal numbers to express twice a given number (in the poets very freq., but not in prose): bis mille sagittae,; so : bis sex, Varr. ap. Prob. Lion.; : bis quinque viri,; ; ; : bis trium ulnarum toga,: duo,: centum, and 209; 12, 188: quattuor,: sex,; 6, 571; 4, 220; 12, 553; 12, 554; 15, 39: septem,: novem, al.—
Bis terve, two or three times, very rarely: a te bis terve summum et eas perbrevis (litteras) accepi,: quem bis terve bonum cum risu miror,.—
Bis terque, several times, repeatedly, ; cf.: stulte bis terque,utterly,. —
Bis tanto or tantum, twice as great, twice as much: bis tanto amici sunt inter se quam prius,; ; : bis tantum quam tuus fundus reddit,: Tartarus ipse Bis patet in praeceps tantum, quantus, etc.,.—
Bis ad eundem (sc.: lapidem offendi, as in ); prov.,to commit the same error twice,.—
Bis minus, in an old enigma in , whose solution is Terminus (ter-minus): semel minusne an bis minus, non sat scio: at utrumque eorum, ut quondam audivi dicier, Jovi ipsi regi noluit concedere.!*? In composition, bis, like the Gr. δίς, loses the s: biceps, bidens, bifer, bigener, bijugus, bilix, etc.; hence bissenus,; ; ; and bisseni,; , and , are better written as two words: bis senus (seni); so either bisextus, or as two words, bis sextus (); v. bisextus.

senses: to binate, to celebrate Mass twice in one day

la:adj:bimus.html:
bīmus, a, um, adj.
prob. contracted from bis-hiems, of two winters; cf. Eutych. ap. P., and Aufrecht, Zeitschrift für vergl. Sprachf. 4, p. 415
,
two years old, of two years, continuing two years: nuces,; : una veterana legio, altera bima, octo tironum, Planc. ap. ; so, semen,: surculi,: plantae,biennial,: merum, * : nix,: pensio,: honor,: aestimatio ususfructus,: si legatum sit relictum annua, bima, trima die, etc., i. e. solvendum intra annum, biennium, triennium, etc.,; cf. dies.—*
In epist. style, as an abbreviated expression: bima sententia,the vote concerning the continuance of a provincial government for two years,.

bis - lingua

Lit., having two tongues; humorously, of voluptuous persons kissing, ; cf. .—
Transf.
Tibiae, with two keys, Varr. ap. .—
Speaking two languages: bilinguis δίγλωσσος, Gloss.: bilingues Bruttates Ennius dixit, quod Bruttii et Osce et Graece loqui soliti sint, Paul. ex Müll.; cf. : corvinus, Canusini more bilinguis,: sed jam bilingues erant, paulatim a domestico externo sermone degeneres,.—

Double-tongued, hypocritical, deceitful, false, treacherous: tamquam proserpens bestia, est bilinguis et scelestus,: edico prius, Ne duplicis habeatis linguas, ne ego bilinguis vos necem, (cf. : bisulcilingua quasi proserpens bestia): quippe domum timet ambiguam Tyriosque bilinguis,: homo,; : os,: socii,: insidiae,.—

la:noun:bibliotheca.html:
biblĭŏthēca (also bī^blĭŏthēcē, ; ;
and BYBL-,; ; ), ae, f., = βιβλιοθήκη, a library; and, as in Greek and English, both a library-room and a collection of books, . The expl. of Isidorus applies to the first signif.: bibliotheca est locus, ubi reponuntur libri, βίβλος enim Graece liber, θήκη repositorium dicitur, ; cf. ; 6, 3, 1. The first public library at Rome was collected by Asinius Pollio A.U.C. 715, B.C. 39, in the atrium of the Temple of Liberty,; ; ; ; . Augustus founded two others, the Octavian, named after his sister Octavia, A.U.C. 721, B.C. 33, near the Theatre of Marcellus, Plut. Vit. Marcell.; and 69 Jahn; and five years after, the Palatine (Gr. and Lat.) Library, on the Palatine Hill, in the Temple of Apollo,; ; Dio, 53, 1; and 41. Besides these there were other considerable libraries in Rome, e. g. in the Temple of Peace, ; in the house of Tiberius,; but esp. one founded by Trajan,, and united by Diocletian with his Thermis, . Individuals also possessed large libraries, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Plut. Lucull.; ; ; ; esp. at their country-seats,; ; —The books were arranged in cases or on shelves along the walls (armaria, foruli, loculamenta, capsae).—The librarian, or person who had the charge of the books, was called a bibliothecā, and 41, or bibliothecarius, v. Dict. of Antiq.
